claim: The ventral posterior hypothalamus (VPH) is implicated in arousal, reproduction, energy balance, and memory processing.
source: The ventral posterior hypothalamus (VPH) is an anatomically complex brain region implicated in arousal, reproduction, energy balance, and memory processing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general characterization of VPH function, drawing on established scientific knowledge about this brain region.

claim: Analysis of >16,000 single cells revealed 20 neuronal and 18 non-neuronal cell populations in the mouse VPH.
source: Analysis of >16,000 single cells revealed 20 neuronal and 18 non-neuronal cell populations, defined by suites of discriminatory markers.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the scRNA-seq analysis presented in the manuscript, supported by experimental data.

claim: The mammillary bodies (MB) are a discrete diencephalic structure on the basal surface of the VPH.
source: The ventral posterior hypothalamus (VPH) is a functionally and cytoarchitecturally complex region of the hypothalamus, dominated by the mammillary bodies (MB), a discrete diencephalic structure on the basal surface of the VPH.
evidence: This is an anatomical description based on established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: The MB are the diencephalic branch of the classic limbic Circuit of Papez.
source: The MB are best known as the diencephalic branch of the classic limbic Circuit of Papez (Papez, 1937), which links the hippocampal formation with the anterior thalamus and midbrain/pons, and is critical for spatial memory in both rodent and primate models, as well as episodic memory in humans (Vann and Aggleton, 2004; Vann, 2010; Aggleton et al., 2010; Dillingham et al., 2015; Vann and Nelson, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature establishing the role of MB in the Circuit of Papez.

claim: The MB are critical for spatial memory in rodent and primate models and episodic memory in humans.
source: The MB are best known as the diencephalic branch of the classic limbic Circuit of Papez (Papez, 1937), which links the hippocampal formation with the anterior thalamus and midbrain/pons, and is critical for spatial memory in both rodent and primate models, as well as episodic memory in humans (Vann and Aggleton, 2004; Vann, 2010; Aggleton et al., 2010; Dillingham et al., 2015; Vann and Nelson, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research on MB function in memory.

claim: The ventral and dorsal PM nuclei are implicated in reproductive and defensive behaviors, respectively.
source: The ventral and dorsal PM nuclei are implicated in reproductive and defensive behaviors, respectively (Canteras et al., 2008; Donato and Elias, 2011; Leshan and Pfaff, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on PM nuclei function.

claim: The SUM is associated with arousal and modulation of theta rhythms.
source: The SUM is associated with arousal and modulation of theta rhythms (Luppi et al., 2017; Pan and McNaughton, 2004; Vertes, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on SUM function.

claim: The Arc is a crucial node in the regulation of hunger, satiety, and reproduction.
source: The Arc is a crucial node in the regulation of hunger, satiety, and reproduction (Graebner et al., 2015; Andermann and Lowell, 2017; Lehman et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on Arc function.

claim: The TMN, populated by histamine-synthesizing neurons, is an important modulator of wakefulness.
source: Finally, the TMN, populated by histamine (HA)-synthesizing neurons, is an important modulator of wakefulness (Brown et al., 2001; Haas et al., 2008; Panula and Nuutinen, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on TMN function.

claim: Single cells were isolated from the VPH of five male and five female C57BL/6 mice (P30-34).
source: To isolate single cells from the mouse VPH for scRNA-seq analysis, we microdissected the region of the VPH from fresh brain slices obtained from a total of five male and five female C57BL/6 mice (P30-34), as described previously (Mickelsen et al., 2017; Mickelsen et al., 2019), in two separate harvests (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: The median transcripts (UMIs)/cell was 8,336 and the median genes/cell was 3,415.
source: In our pooled data set, the median transcripts (UMIs)/cell was 8,336 and the median genes/cell was 3,415 (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the scRNA-seq data analysis, shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Neuronal and non-neuronal clusters were segregated using a two-component Gaussian mixture model trained on the per-cluster average expression of four pan-neuronal markers Snap25, Syp, Tubb3, and Elavl2.
source: Neuronal and non-neuronal clusters were segregated using a two-component Gaussian mixture model trained on the per-cluster average expression of four pan-neuronal markers Snap25, Syp, Tubb3, and Elavl2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,c) leading to a binary classification of neuronal and non-neuronal cells (Figure 1e,f).
evidence: This describes the computational method used to classify cells, with results shown in figures.

claim: Among non-neuronal cell populations in the VPH, 18 distinct clusters were identified.
source: Among non-neuronal cell populations in the VPH, we identified 18 distinct clusters distinguished from one another by suites of cell type-specific discriminatory markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a–d).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of non-neuronal cells, supported by data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Six distinct populations of oligodendrocyte lineage cells were resolved, including oligodendrocyte precursor cells, immature oligodendrocytes, and four oligodendrocyte populations.
source: We resolved six distinct populations of oligodendrocyte lineage cells arranged in a contiguous strand in a UMAP plot (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a), likely reflecting a developmental gradient of gene expression. These include oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPC or NG2+ cells; cluster 1), immature oligodendrocytes (cluster 2), and four oligodendrocyte populations (clusters 3–6), all of which exhibit a wave of differentially-expressed genes (Cspg4, Fyn, Ctps, Tspans2, Apod, Klk6, etc.; Figure 1—figure supplement 5a and b) that aligns well with the diversity of functional markers of the oligodendrocyte lineage in the mouse brain identified through previous scRNA-seq analyses (Marques et al., 2016; Zeisel et al., 2018; Saunders et al., 2018).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in supplementary figures and is consistent with previous scRNA-seq studies cited.

claim: Three distinct clusters of astrocytes were resolved, all of which are Aqp4+ and Agt+.
source: We also resolved three distinct clusters of astrocytes (clusters 7, 8, and 9), all of which are Aqp4+ and Agt+.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of non-neuronal cells, based on marker gene expression.

claim: Of the 20 neuronal clusters identified, thirteen are glutamatergic, six are GABAergic and one is histaminergic.
source: We found that of the 20 neuronal clusters we identified, thirteen are glutamatergic, six are GABAergic and one (cluster 17) best matched the profile of a unique population of histaminergic (HA) neurons based on the unique expression of histidine decarboxylase (Hdc/HDC; Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is a classification of neuronal clusters based on neurotransmitter phenotype, supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2.

claim: VPHGLUT cluster 7 is enriched in Tac1, Nos1, Calb2, and Foxp2 and corresponds to the ventral premammillary nucleus (PMv).
source: Among neuronal clusters that correspond to discrete anatomical subregions of the VPH, we identified at least one VPHGLUT population with a suite of differentially-expressed transcripts that appears to closely match the ventral premammillary nucleus (PMv; Figure 3). VPHGLUT cluster 7 is enriched in the following key transcripts: Tac1 (encoding substance P or SP), Nos1 (encoding neuronal nitric oxide synthase or NOS), Calb2 (encoding calretinin), and Foxp2 (encoding the transcription factor forkhead box P2; Figure 3a) along with a host of other differentially expressed markers (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis, mapping a transcriptional cluster to an anatomical region, supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: The spatial pattern of expression of Tac1, Nos1, Calb2, and Foxp2 in the Allen Brain Atlas corresponds closely to the PMv.
source: The spatial pattern of expression of each of the markers in Figure 3a were found in the ABA (Lein et al., 2007), and correspond closely to the PMv (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with ISH data from the Allen Brain Atlas, shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Tac1, Calb2, and Slc17a6 are extensively co-expressed in a large cluster of neurons in the PMv.
source: Through FISH co-expression analysis, we found that Tac1, Calb2, and Slc17a6 are extensively co-expressed in a large cluster of neurons in the PMv (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from FISH validation experiments, with data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: A distinct subpopulation of VPHGLUT cluster 7 neurons robustly expresses markers of catecholaminergic neurotransmission including Slc6a3, Ddc, and Slc18a2 but low expression of Th.
source: Interestingly, we also found that a distinct subpopulation of VPHGLUT cluster 7 neurons robustly expresses markers of catecholaminergic neurotransmission including Slc6a3 (encoding the dopamine transporter, DAT), Ddc (encoding DOPA decarboxylase), and Slc18a2 (encoding the vesicular monoamine transporter 2, VMAT2) but low expression of Th (encoding tyrosine hydroxylase; Figure 3e).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis identifying a subpopulation with a specific molecular profile, shown in Figure 3e.

claim: This cluster corresponds well to a previously identified catecholaminergic, Slc6a3+ PMv population.
source: This cluster corresponds well to a previously identified catcholaminergic (Zoli et al., 1993), Slc6a3+ PMv population (Meister and Elde, 1993) that was more recently found, through circuit and behavioral analyses, to regulate male social behavior (Soden et al., 2016) and aggression (Stagkourakis et al., 2018) in a glutamate-dependent, but dopamine-independent, manner (Soden et al., 2016), consistent with the profile we identified (Slc17a6+, Slc18a2+, Slc6a3+, Ddc+, Th-).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies that identified and characterized this PMv population.

claim: VPHGLUT cluster 6 expresses Cck, Foxb1, Synpr, Dlk1, Ebf3, and Stxbp6 and likely represents a PMd population.
source: Another distinct VPHGLUT population (cluster 6) share a number of common markers with clusters 1–5, for example Cck (encoding the neuropeptide cholecystokinin) and Foxb1 (encoding the transcription factor Forkhead Box B1), which are largely undetectable in clusters 7–10 (Figure 4a,b). Curiously, VPHGLUT cluster 6 also expresses a suite of markers that are enriched in clusters 7–10 (ex. Ebf3, Dlk1, Synpr, Nxph1) but largely undetectable in clusters 1–5 (Figure 4a,b). In particular, Synpr (encoding the presynaptic protein synaptoporin), Dlk1 (encoding delta like non-canonical Notch ligand 1), Ebf3 (encoding early B cell factor 3) and Stxbp6 (encoding the synaptic protein syntaxin binding protein 6) are enriched in VPHGLUT cluster 6 (Figure 4a,b). Examining the expression patterns of Synpr, Dlk1, and Stxbp6 in the ABA (Lein et al., 2007), we found that all three are enriched in a discrete region that appears to correspond well to the dorsal PM (PMd; Figure 4c,d) and are largely undetectable in the more caudal mammillary bodies (MB; Figure 4d). This suggests that VPHGLUT cluster 6 likely represents a PMd population that expresses a number of unique signatures (ex. Synpr, Stxbp6) but shares some commonalities with VPHGLUT clusters 1–5 (ex. Foxb1, Cck, Adcyap1) and VPHGLUT cluster 7, a putative PMv population (ex. Nxph1, Ar).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis, mapping a transcriptional cluster to the PMd based on marker gene expression patterns in the Allen Brain Atlas.

claim: VPHGLUT cluster 8 corresponds to the supramammillary (SUM) nuclei.
source: Another notable neuronal cluster is VPHGLUT cluster 8. Subjecting this cluster to another iteration of unsupervised clustering revealed six subclusters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a) which exhibit suites of differentially expressed genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,c). Several of the markers that define distinct subclusters within VPHGLUT cluster 8 are found within anatomically identified neuronal populations in the SUM (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d), only the most ventral portion of which would be included in our microdissection (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis, mapping cluster 8 to the SUM based on marker gene expression.

claim: At least one subpopulation of VPHGLUT cluster 8 appears to co-express Slc17a6, Slc32a1, and Gad2 but not Gad1.
source: Although all cells in cluster 8 express Slc17a6, and are nominally classified as glutamatergic, at least one subpopulation appears to co-express Slc32a1 and Gad2 but not Gad1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis identifying a dual phenotype subpopulation, shown in supplementary figures.

claim: A unique population of VGLUT2/VGAT co-expressing axons originating in the SUM has been described among projections to the hippocampal dentate gyrus.
source: Interestingly, a unique population of VGLUT2/VGAT co-expressing axons originating in the SUM has been described among projections to the hippocampal dentate gyrus (Boulland et al., 2009; Soussi et al., 2010) and these dual phenotype SUM neurons were found to indeed co-release GABA and glutamate onto neurons of the dentate gyrus (Pedersen et al., 2017; Hashimotodani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies that identified dual phenotype SUM neurons.

claim: VPHGLUT cluster 16 expresses Tac2, Pdyn, and Esr1 and corresponds to Arc KNDy neurons.
source: A highly distinct neuronal cluster, VPHGLUT cluster 16, which did not subcluster further, expresses a suite of markers that identify it as a well-described neuronal cell type in the Arc - kisspeptin-neurokinin B-dynorphin (KNDy) neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2f). KNDy neurons are considered to be the gonadotropin-releasing hormone pulse generator controlling release of luteinizing hormone from the anterior pituitary, and therefore essential for fertility and reproduction (Lehman et al., 2010; Moore et al., 2018; Harter et al., 2018). We confirm that this cluster co-expresses the defining neuropeptides Tac2 (encoding neurokinin B) and Pdyn (encoding dynorphin; Figure 4—figure supplement 2c,f).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis identifying KNDy neurons, supported by marker gene expression and citations to previous research on KNDy neuron function.

claim: VPHHA cluster 17 neurons express Hdc, Slc18a2, Maob, and Wif1 and correspond to histaminergic neurons in the tuberomammillary nuclei.
source: A highly distinct cluster emerged from our data set that exhibits a pattern of gene expression characteristic of histamine (HA)-producing neurons (VPHHA cluster 17). HA neurons are a well-characterized monoaminergic, neuromodulatory population with cell bodies concentrated in the ventral TMN (TMNv) and dorsal TMN (TMNd), and also scattered throughout the VPH region. TMN HA neurons are the sole source of neuronally-synthesized HA in the brain, make widespread projections throughout the brain (Ericson et al., 1987; Inagaki et al., 1988) and have a key role in modulating wakefulness (Brown et al., 2001; Haas et al., 2008; Panula and Nuutinen, 2013). Previous mouse hypothalamic scRNA-seq studies have also detected a population of HA neurons (Chen et al., 2017; Campbell et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2020). We found that VPHHA cluster 17 neurons express the following key transcripts: Hdc, in addition to Slc18a2 (encoding the vesicular monoamine transporter two or VMAT2), Maob (encoding monoamine oxidase B), and another unique marker Wif1 (encoding Wnt inhibitory factor 1; Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis identifying histaminergic neurons, supported by marker gene expression and citations to previous research.

claim: FISH analysis revealed extensive co-expression of Wif1 and Maob with Hdc in both the TMNv and TMNd.
source: FISH analysis of Wif1 and Maob co-expression with Hdc revealed extensive co-expression in both the TMNv and TMNd but with lower coexpression in the TMNd (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is a finding from FISH validation experiments, with data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: VPHHA cluster 17 neurons robustly co-express Gad1 accompanied by very low co-expression of Slc32a1.
source: With regard to fast neurotransmitter phenotype, we found that VPHHA cluster 17 neurons are exceptional in our data set in that they express very low levels of both Slc17a6 and Slc32a1, but robustly express Gad1. That TMN HA neurons are GAD+, and likely capable of GABA synthesis, has long been recognized (Vincent et al., 1983; Takeda et al., 1984). While there has been recent conflicting data on whether or not HA neurons express Slc32a1 (Yu et al., 2015; Venner et al., 2019), our data indicate that TMN HA neurons robustly co-express Gad1 accompanied by very low co-expression of Slc32a1.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis regarding the neurotransmitter phenotype of HA neurons, with reference to previous conflicting data.

claim: VPHGLUT cluster 20 is characterized by the expression of Tac2, Pvalb, Cplx1, and Tcf4 and corresponds to the lateral mammillary (LM) nuclei.
source: We identified a distinct VPHGLUT population (cluster 20) characterized by the expression of Tac2, Pvalb (encoding the calcium-binding protein parvalbumin), Cplx1 (encoding the synaptic protein complexin-1), and Tcf4 (encoding transcription factor 4; Figure 6a), in addition to a suite of other discriminatory markers including Fgf1, Cbln2, Infg2, Nefm, Myo1a, and Syt2 (Figure 6b). The spatial pattern of expression of Tac2, Pvalb, Cplx1, and Tcf4 in the ABA (Lein et al., 2007) corresponds well to the lateral mammillary (LM) nuclei, which are tightly circumscribed bilateral cell clusters, immediately lateral to the medial mammillary region and bisected by the fornix (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis, mapping cluster 20 to the LM based on marker gene expression patterns in the Allen Brain Atlas.

claim: LM neurons are components of the MB and are implicated in the encoding of head direction and aspects of spatial memory.
source: LM neurons are components of the MB and are implicated in the encoding of head direction and aspects of spatial memory (Vann and Aggleton, 2004; Dillingham et al., 2015; Dillingham and Vann, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on LM neuron function.

claim: FISH analysis revealed extensive co-expression of Tac2, Pvalb, Cplx1, and Tcf4 with Slc17a6 in the LM.
source: Consistent with our scRNA-seq results, FISH analysis revealed extensive co-expression of Tac2, Pvalb, Cplx1, and Tcf4 with Slc17a6 in the LM.
evidence: This is a finding from FISH validation experiments confirming the scRNA-seq results.

claim: Pvalb expression is limited to a subset of Slc17a6+ neurons in the LM.
source: Notably, Pvalb expression is limited to a subset of Slc17a6+ neurons in the LM (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is a finding from FISH experiments, shown in Figure 6d.

claim: VPHGLUT clusters 1–5 share common markers including Cartpt, Cck, Adcyap1, and Foxb1 and correspond to the medial mammillary region.
source: We identified five VPHGLUT clusters that appear to be both closely interrelated to each other transcriptionally and distinct from other neuronal clusters. VPHGLUT clusters 1–5 are arranged in close proximity in UMAP space (Figure 2b), with clusters 1 and 2 forming one contiguous cluster and clusters 3–5 forming another. Clusters 1–5 share a number of common markers including genes that encode the neuropeptides Cartpt, Cck, Adcyap1 as well as the transcription factor Foxb1 (Figure 7a,b). Cross-referencing Cartpt, Foxb1, Cck, and Adcyap1 with the ABA (Lein et al., 2007) indicate that VPHGLUT clusters 1–5 correspond well to the medial mammillary region (Figure 7c), which itself may be subdivided into cytoarchitecturally-defined anatomical compartments: median (MnM), medial (MM), and lateral (ML) subdivisions (Paxinos, 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis, mapping clusters 1-5 to the medial mammillary region based on shared marker gene expression.

claim: Multiplex FISH analysis revealed extensive co-expression of Cck, Adcyap1, and Cartpt with Slc17a6 in the medial mammillary region.
source: Multiplex FISH analysis revealed extensive co-expression of the neuropeptide transcripts Cck, Adcyap1, and Cartpt with Slc17a6 in the region (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is a finding from FISH validation experiments, with data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Transcriptionally distinct medial mammillary subpopulations exhibit spatial segregation within the MnM, MM, and ML subdivisions.
source: We further investigated differentially expressed genes among VPHGLUT clusters 1–5 (Figure 8a), that comprise the medial mammillary region in an effort to determine if they exhibit any spatial organization with respect to the cytoarchitecurally-defined MnM, MM, and ML subdivisions. We identified a suite of differentially-expressed genes that define each of the transcriptionally distinct medial mammillary clusters 1–5 (Figure 8b) with two discriminatory genes from each shown in UMAP plots (Figure 8c). We went on to cross reference these makers with their spatial distribution within the medial mammillary region using the ABA (Lein et al., 2007) and found striking patterns of segmentation.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq analysis showing spatial organization of transcriptionally distinct populations within the medial mammillary region.

claim: Markers for cluster 1 neurons (Nts+, Col25a1+) appear to be enriched in the MM subdivision.
source: Markers for cluster 1 neurons (Nts+, Col25a1+) appear to be enriched in the MM subdivision, medial to the principle mammillary tract (pm), whereas markers for cluster 4 neurons (Nos1+, Calb1+) are found concentrated in the ML subdivision, lateral to the principle mammillary tract (pm) and medial to the fornix (f).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing scRNA-seq marker gene expression with spatial patterns in the Allen Brain Atlas.

claim: Markers for cluster 4 neurons (Nos1+, Calb1+) are found concentrated in the ML subdivision.
source: Markers for cluster 1 neurons (Nts+, Col25a1+) appear to be enriched in the MM subdivision, medial to the principle mammillary tract (pm), whereas markers for cluster 4 neurons (Nos1+, Calb1+) are found concentrated in the ML subdivision, lateral to the principle mammillary tract (pm) and medial to the fornix (f).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing scRNA-seq marker gene expression with spatial patterns in the Allen Brain Atlas.

claim: Cluster 2 neurons (Gpr83+, Spock3+) are concentrated in the central portion of the MnM subdivision.
source: Cluster 2 neurons (Gpr83+, Spock3+) are concentrated in the central portion of the MnM subdivision, whereas cluster 3 neurons (Pvalb+, Slc24a2+) are enriched in the more dorsal portion of the MnM.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing scRNA-seq marker gene expression with spatial patterns in the Allen Brain Atlas.

claim: Cluster 3 neurons (Pvalb+, Slc24a2+) are enriched in the more dorsal portion of the MnM.
source: Cluster 2 neurons (Gpr83+, Spock3+) are concentrated in the central portion of the MnM subdivision, whereas cluster 3 neurons (Pvalb+, Slc24a2+) are enriched in the more dorsal portion of the MnM.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing scRNA-seq marker gene expression with spatial patterns in the Allen Brain Atlas.

claim: Cluster 5 neurons (Tac2+, Cxcl14+) appear to correspond to a thin rim of small diameter neurons on the basal surface of the MM and ML.
source: Interestingly, cluster 5 neurons (Tac2+, Cxcl14+) appear to correspond to a thin rim of small diameter, Tac2+ neurons hugging the basal surface of the MM and ML (Figure 8d), overlapping with the region typically referred to as the TMNv or VTM (Paxinos, 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing scRNA-seq marker gene expression with spatial patterns in the Allen Brain Atlas.

claim: Neurons in the MB make a major, unidirectional projection to the anterior thalamic nuclei (ATN) through the mammillothalamic tract (mtt).
source: Neurons in the MB make two highly specific projections in the brain: (1) a major, unidirectional projection to the anterior thalamic nuclei (ATN) through the mammillothalamic tract (mtt); and (2) a bidirectional connection to the ventral tegmental nucleus of Gudden (VTg), via the mamillotegmental tract (mtg) (summarized in Figure 9c; Vann and Aggleton, 2004; Vann, 2010; Aggleton et al., 2010; Dillingham et al., 2015; Vann and Nelson, 2015).
evidence: This is an established anatomical fact about MB projections, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neurons in the MB make a bidirectional connection to the ventral tegmental nucleus of Gudden (VTg), via the mamillotegmental tract (mtg).
source: Neurons in the MB make two highly specific projections in the brain: (1) a major, unidirectional projection to the anterior thalamic nuclei (ATN) through the mammillothalamic tract (mtt); and (2) a bidirectional connection to the ventral tegmental nucleus of Gudden (VTg), via the mamillotegmental tract (mtg) (summarized in Figure 9c; Vann and Aggleton, 2004; Vann, 2010; Aggleton et al., 2010; Dillingham et al., 2015; Vann and Nelson, 2015).
evidence: This is an established anatomical fact about MB projections, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The MM projects topographically to the AM, the ML to the AV and the LM to the AD.
source: In particular, the MM projects topographically to the AM, the ML to the AV and the LM to the AD (Aggleton et al., 2010; Shibata, 1992; Jankowski et al., 2013; Bubb et al., 2017; Seki and Zyo, 1984; Hayakawa and Zyo, 1989; Wright et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an established anatomical fact about topographic MB-ATN projections, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Using the Slc17a6 (VGLUT2)-Cre driver line to broadly target VPHGLUT neurons in the MB, labeling was found throughout the medial mammillary region but largely sparing the LM.
source: Using the Slc17a6 (VGLUT2)-Cre driver line to broadly target VPHGLUT neurons in the MB and their projections, we found labeling throughout the medial mammillary region at the injection site (Figure 9e), but largely sparing the LM, shown in a representative mouse.
evidence: This is a finding from anterograde tracing experiments, with data shown in Figure 9e.

claim: Slc17a6-Cre labeled axons were observed in the mtt, mtg, VTg, and a high density of fibers in the AV and AM of the ATN, but not AD.
source: In addition to finding a high density of labeled axons in the mtt and mtg, we observed a plexus of fibers in the VTg and a high density of fibers in much of the ATN (AV and AM, but not AD, consistent with the latter being the target of LM projections).
evidence: This is a finding from anterograde tracing experiments using Slc17a6-Cre mice.

claim: Using the Nts-Cre line to selectively target VPHGLUT cluster 1 neurons, the AM subdivision of the ATN appeared to be selectively targeted, while sparing the AV and AD.
source: Next, using the Nts-Cre line to selectively target VPHGLUT cluster 1 neurons, that we had previously mapped to the MM subdivision, we found labeling at the injection site between the MM and ML and labeled axons in the mtt, mtg, and VTg, shown in a representative mouse. However, in the ATN, the AM subdivision appeared to be selectively targeted, while sparing the AV and AD (Figure 9e).
evidence: This is a finding from anterograde tracing experiments using Nts-Cre mice, with data shown in Figure 9e.

claim: Using the Calb1-Cre driver to target VPHGLUT cluster 4 neurons, highly specific labeling of the AV subdivision of the ATN was observed, while sparing the AM and AD.
source: Finally, using the Calb1-Cre driver to target VPHGLUT cluster 4 neurons, that we had mapped to the ML subdivision, we found clear labeling in the ML at the injection site (with some weak labeling in the MM/MnM) and labeled axons in the mtt, mtg, and VTg, shown in a representative mouse. Interestingly, and in stark contrast to our Nts-cre results, we observed highly specific labeling of the AV subdivision of the ATN, while sparing the AM and AD.
evidence: This is a finding from anterograde tracing experiments using Calb1-Cre mice.

claim: Molecularly-defined subpopulations of MB neurons are highly segregated within the anatomical subdivisions of the MB and project to distinct domains within the ATN.
source: Taken together, these anterograde tracing data suggest that not only are molecularly-defined subpopulations of MB neurons highly segregated within the anatomical subdivisions of the MB (MnM, MM, ML, and LM), but these subpopulations appear to project to distinct domains within the ATN, consistent with previous anterograde and retrograde tracing data without genetic specificity (Aggleton et al., 2010; Shibata, 1992; Jankowski et al., 2013; Bubb et al., 2017; Seki and Zyo, 1984; Hayakawa and Zyo, 1989; Wright et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anterograde tracing experiments, consistent with previous anatomical studies.

claim: Foxb1-null mice exhibit dysgenesis of both the MB and mtt and display defects in spatial memory tasks.
source: For example, Foxb1 is well-known to define the MB during early embryonic development (Shimogori et al., 2010; Kaestner et al., 1996; Wehr et al., 1997; Radyushkin et al., 2005) and Foxb1-null mice exhibit dysgenesis of both the MB and mtt (Wehr et al., 1997; Radyushkin et al., 2005; Alvarez-Bolado et al., 2000) and display defects in spatial memory tasks, particularly spatial navigation and working memory (Radyushkin et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Foxb1 function in MB development and spatial memory.

claim: Gpr83-null mice exhibit impaired spatial learning.
source: Furthermore, the enrichment of the recently deorphanized receptor Gpr83 (Gomes et al., 2016) that we observed in this region (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1) aligns with previous anatomical work showing high expression in the MB (Pesini et al., 1998) and behavioral experiments showing that Gpr83-null mice also exhibit impaired spatial learning (Vollmer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Gpr83 expression and function in spatial learning.

claim: The MB may have a key role in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's Disease (AD).
source: Finally, given the important and conserved role of the MB as a node in a brain-wide memory system and multiple aspects of spatial and episodic memory, it is significant that the MB may have a key role in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's Disease (AD). Evidence from imaging of AD patients and postmortem examination of AD-afflicted brains suggest that the MB, fornix, and mtt all show varying degrees of atrophy or degeneration that may be correlated with cognitive decline and memory loss (Callen et al., 2001; Copenhaver et al., 2006; Grossi et al., 1989; Baloyannis et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous clinical and postmortem studies on AD pathology.

claim: The MB was identified as among the earliest sites of beta-amyloid deposition in the brain of 5XFAD mice, appearing as early as two months after birth.
source: Recent work has implicated the MB and other components of the Papez circuit as sites of particular vulnerability in the pathogenesis of AD in mice (Canter et al., 2019). Using a quantitative measure of beta-amyloid deposition in the whole brain of 5XFAD mice, a mouse model of AD (Oakley et al., 2006), the MB was identified as among the earliest sites of beta-amyloid deposition in the brain, appearing as early as two months after birth.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study on AD pathology in a mouse model.

claim: TMN HA neurons exhibit dramatic loss in post mortem AD-afflicted brains.
source: In addition, other VPH subpopulations may exhibit selective vulnerability in AD as evidenced by the presence of AD pathological features in the TMN and dramatic loss of TMN HA neurons in post mortem AD-afflicted brains (Saper and German, 1987; Airaksinen et al., 1991; Nakamura et al., 1993; Oh et al., 2019), likely contributing to sleep-wake disturbances commonly observed in AD patients (Spira et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous postmortem studies on TMN pathology in AD.

claim: The cluster classifier can predict neuronal cluster identity with over 90% accuracy with fewer than 80 total genes.
source: This computational experiment demonstrates that we can predict the neuronal cluster identity with over 90% accuracy with fewer than only 80 total genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b–d).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational validation of marker gene specificity, with results shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Neuronal cells contained significantly more genes and UMIs per cell (4334 and 12,065, respectively) than the overall data set.
source: Among the neuronal clusters, which contained significantly more genes and UMIs per cell (4334 and 12,065, respectively) than the overall data set, we first examined broad patterns in the expression of fast amino acid and monoamine neurotransmitter markers (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis comparing neuronal and overall cell populations.

claim: The identification of oligodendrocyte lineage cells aligns well with the diversity of functional markers identified through previous scRNA-seq analyses.
source: These include oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPC or NG2+ cells; cluster 1), immature oligodendrocytes (cluster 2), and four oligodendrocyte populations (clusters 3–6), all of which exhibit a wave of differentially-expressed genes (Cspg4, Fyn, Ctps, Tspans2, Apod, Klk6, etc.; Figure 1—figure supplement 5a and b) that aligns well with the diversity of functional markers of the oligodendrocyte lineage in the mouse brain identified through previous scRNA-seq analyses (Marques et al., 2016; Zeisel et al., 2018; Saunders et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with previous scRNA-seq studies cited.

claim: The identification of major non-neuronal VPH cell types is based on and closely aligns with previous scRNA-seq analyses from mouse brain.
source: Our identification of major non-neuronal VPH cell types is based on, and closely aligns with, previous scRNA-seq analyses from mouse brain (Marques et al., 2016; Zeisel et al., 2018; Saunders et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous scRNA-seq studies.

claim: PACAP+ PMv neurons critically regulate female reproductive physiology and fertility.
source: Another marker that is enriched in VPHGLUT cluster 7 is Adcyap1 (encoding the neuropeptide pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide, or PACAP; Figure 3b). Consistent with the role of the PMv in reproductive function (Donato and Elias, 2011; Leshan and Pfaff, 2014), PACAP+ PMv neurons were recently shown to critically regulate female reproductive physiology and fertility (Ross et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study on PACAP+ PMv neuron function.

claim: A previously identified Slc6a3+ PMv population regulates male social behavior and aggression in a glutamate-dependent, but dopamine-independent, manner.
source: This cluster corresponds well to a previously identified catcholaminergic (Zoli et al., 1993), Slc6a3+ PMv population (Meister and Elde, 1993) that was more recently found, through circuit and behavioral analyses, to regulate male social behavior (Soden et al., 2016) and aggression (Stagkourakis et al., 2018) in a glutamate-dependent, but dopamine-independent, manner (Soden et al., 2016), consistent with the profile we identified (Slc17a6+, Slc18a2+, Slc6a3+, Ddc+, Th-).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on the function of this PMv population.

claim: Dual phenotype SUM neurons co-release GABA and glutamate onto neurons of the dentate gyrus.
source: Interestingly, a unique population of VGLUT2/VGAT co-expressing axons originating in the SUM has been described among projections to the hippocampal dentate gyrus (Boulland et al., 2009; Soussi et al., 2010) and these dual phenotype SUM neurons were found to indeed co-release GABA and glutamate onto neurons of the dentate gyrus (Pedersen et al., 2017; Hashimotodani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on dual phenotype SUM neurons.

claim: KNDy neurons are considered to be the gonadotropin-releasing hormone pulse generator controlling release of luteinizing hormone from the anterior pituitary.
source: KNDy neurons are considered to be the gonadotropin-releasing hormone pulse generator controlling release of luteinizing hormone from the anterior pituitary, and therefore essential for fertility and reproduction (Lehman et al., 2010; Moore et al., 2018; Harter et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on KNDy neuron function.

claim: TMN HA neurons are the sole source of neuronally-synthesized HA in the brain.
source: TMN HA neurons are the sole source of neuronally-synthesized HA in the brain, make widespread projections throughout the brain (Ericson et al., 1987; Inagaki et al., 1988) and have a key role in modulating wakefulness (Brown et al., 2001; Haas et al., 2008; Panula and Nuutinen, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on HA neuron anatomy and function.

claim: TMN HA neurons have a key role in modulating wakefulness.
source: TMN HA neurons are the sole source of neuronally-synthesized HA in the brain, make widespread projections throughout the brain (Ericson et al., 1987; Inagaki et al., 1988) and have a key role in modulating wakefulness (Brown et al., 2001; Haas et al., 2008; Panula and Nuutinen, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on HA neuron function in wakefulness.

claim: TMN HA neurons are GAD+ and likely capable of GABA synthesis.
source: That TMN HA neurons are GAD+, and likely capable of GABA synthesis, has long been recognized (Vincent et al., 1983; Takeda et al., 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on HA neuron neurochemistry.

claim: The AM is uniquely interconnected with the prelimbic cortex and thought to have a role in relaying information from the hippocampal formation and MB to prefrontal cortical centers.
source: For example, aside from reciprocal connections with the anterior cingulate, the AM is uniquely interconnected with the prelimbic cortex, and thought to have a role in relaying information from the hippocampal formation and MB to prefrontal cortical centers associated with higher cognitive function (Aggleton et al., 2010; Jankowski et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on AM connectivity and function.

claim: The AV is interconnected with the retrosplenial cortex and subiculum and implicated in theta entrainment.
source: The AV, in contrast, is interconnected with the retrosplenial cortex (Shibata and Kato, 1993) and subiculum (Shibata, 1993), and implicated in theta entrainment (Aggleton et al., 2010; Jankowski et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on AV connectivity and function.

claim: Specific lesions to the mtt and VTg, but not to the postcommissural fornix, result in deficits in spatial memory.
source: The importance of MB projections to the ATN and VTg is highlighted by previous work showing that specific lesions to the mtt and VTg, but not to the postcommissural fornix, result in deficits in spatial memory, suggesting that MB-ATN and MB-VTg connectivity have critical roles in memory, likely independent of hippocampal input (Vann, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous lesion studies on MB projection function.

claim: Korsakoff's syndrome is characterized by selective degeneration of the MB and is accompanied by severe amnesia.
source: For example, Korsakoff's syndrome, caused by thiamine deficiency associated with chronic alcoholism, is characterized by selective degeneration of the MB and is accompanied by severe amnesia (Kopelman, 1995; Kril and Harper, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous clinical studies on Korsakoff's syndrome.

claim: Chemogenetic silencing of medial mammillary neurons resulted in reduced beta amyloid deposition in 5XFAD mice.
source: This observation was accompanied by an increase in medial mammillary neuronal excitability, that when chemogenetically silenced, resulted in reduced beta amyloid deposition (Canter et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study on AD pathology in a mouse model.

claim: The VPH cell type census contributes to a more comprehensive picture of the cell type diversity and spatial organization of the mammalian hypothalamus.
source: Overall, our VPH cell type census, along with other recent hypothalamic scRNA-seq analyses (Mickelsen et al., 2019; Moffitt et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2017; Zeisel et al., 2018; Romanov et al., 2017; Campbell et al., 2017; Rossi et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019), contributes to a more comprehensive picture of the cell type diversity and spatial organization of the mammalian hypothalamus, as well as informing the molecular, cellular, and synaptic mechanisms of hypothalamic circuit function in health and disease.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the significance of the work, drawing on the data presented and citing related studies.
